format_note: Repository-native schema. Not claimed to be Anthropic-compatible or any vendor format. Adapt via adapter if needed.
description: Evaluation cases for the Analytics Engineering Skills Repository. Each case asserts expected workflow routing and behavior, and explicitly flags unwanted actions (over-engineering, pointless questions, jumping to solutions). Cases cover both positive (correct) routing and negative (near-miss or anti-pattern) prompts to test restraint.

cases.title: Ambiguous dashboard request
cases.input: Create a sales dashboard for me.
expected_behaviors: Asks high-value clarification questions about persona, decision, KPIs, grain, dimensions, timeframe.
Does not start building charts or writing DAX before business problem is defined.
Converts dashboard request into a decision problem.
expected_not: Does not immediately suggest a stack (Power BI / Tableau / dbt) without understanding context.
Does not start producing a star schema or SQL model in the first response.

cases.title: Why did revenue drop? — Business diagnostic
cases.input: Our revenue decreased 12% WoW. Why?
expected_behaviors: Clarifies scope of revenue (which business line, region, channel, grain).
Confirms data source, freshness, and known changes that week.
Performs segmented and driver-based breakdowns before conclusions.
Distinguishes correlation vs. causation; explicitly calls out assumptions.
expected_not: Does not jump to a single causal story on day 1.
Does not propose ML / forecasting for a root-cause diagnostic.

cases.title: DAX optimization request
cases.input: Optimize this DAX measure: CALCULATE(SUMX(FILTER(ALL(FactSales), FactSales[Region]=MAX(DimRegion[Region])), FactSales[Amount]))
expected_behaviors: Establishes baseline: correctness of current measure (check business logic), then timing/Server Timings baseline.
Identifies bottleneck: FILTER over ALL(entire fact) inside an iterator.
Proposes simpler CALCULATE with filter argument (e.g., via relationship or TREATAS) and benchmarks.
Validates numerical equivalence after optimization.
expected_not: Does not rewrite into a form that changes business semantics (e.g., changing filter context to different grain) without flagging.
Does not claim performance gain without a measured baseline.

cases.title: Duplicate rows in mart
cases.input: Our mart_sales_report has 10x more rows than last week. Users complaining about wrong totals.
expected_behaviors: Bisects: source → bronze → silver → gold → mart to find the first layer producing row count explosion.
Suspects: changed join key, cross-product from missing join condition, upstream batch re-run + append, changed grain.
Tests hypotheses and isolates root cause; distinguishes root cause vs. contributing factors.
Proposes workaround if urgent, then permanent fix; regression checks adjacent slices.
Recommends data-quality checks (uniqueness on grain-defining columns, row-count anomaly alert) to prevent recurrence.
expected_not: Does not add DISTINCT at the top layer as the only fix without root-causing.
Does not blame users or 'bad data' without evidence.

cases.title: Unnecessary ML request (near-miss negative)
cases.input: Use ML to predict our daily sales for next year. Pick the fanciest model.
expected_behaviors: Asks: decision to be supported, required accuracy, baseline (e.g., seasonal naive + last year + moving average), error costs, and value proposition vs. baseline.
Implements non-ML baselines first (seasonal naive, moving average, simple regression).
Only proposes ML if it materially outperforms baselines on the primary metric AND adds business value vs. operation cost.
Explicitly refuses 'pick the fanciest' criterion and explains why.
expected_not: Does not immediately recommend XGBoost/LSTM/neural net because 'ML is best'.
Does not skip baselines.
Does not skip data-science reference progression (descriptive → diagnostic → baseline → predictive).

cases.title: Source reconciliation across two systems
cases.input: Reconcile the revenue numbers between ERP and CRM. They never match.
expected_behaviors: Defines reconciliation dimensions: technical equality vs. semantic equality vs. business equality.
Grain check per source: is revenue per invoice line, per order, per posted day, per recognized-day?
Statuses: what counts in each system (booked, shipped, invoiced, paid?). Timing cutoffs, timezone, returns/credits treatment.
Presents a reconciliation matrix with differences quantified per dimension, and recommends mapping / source-of-truth rules.
expected_not: Does not simply pick one system as 'right' without defining rules.
Does not stop at 'they differ by 4.3%' without explaining drivers.

cases.title: SQL optimization candidate
cases.input: This query runs for 10 minutes on 1B rows, make it faster. [includes a 5-CTE correlated subquery with many SELECT * and implicit joins]
expected_behaviors: Asks for or proposes to capture actual execution plan, timing, IO, and size.
Separates anti-patterns (SELECT *, implicit joins without ON, correlated subqueries rewritable as window functions / joins).
Identifies bottleneck, changes one factor at a time, benchmarks each iteration.
Validates numerical equivalence after rewrite.
expected_not: Does not apply all 'best practices' in a single rewrite, making attribution impossible.
Does not measure only end-to-end time without attributing to plan operations.

cases.title: Power BI dashboard UX check
cases.input: We built this Power BI report. Users say it's confusing and slow. Review it.
expected_behaviors: Applies review workflow across 8 dimensions: business, data, logic, engineering, perf, security, UX, ops.
Checks dashboard UX hierarchy: Context → KPI → Diagnosis → Detail → Action.
Checks visualizations: each answers a question, accessible, no chart junk.
Captures Performance Analyzer baseline, identifies worst visual(s), routes to optimize if > threshold.
expected_not: Does not only say 'make prettier'.
Does not skip performance if slow was explicitly mentioned.

cases.title: Daily pipeline design (operational scenarios)
cases.input: Design and plan the daily pipeline that ingests ERP raw, builds marts, and refreshes Power BI. SLA: marts ready by 07:00.
expected_behaviors: Defines DAG and SLOs. Specifies bronze → silver → gold layers.
Idempotency, incremental, watermark, checkpointing, atomic publish.
Explicit operational scenarios: fails 06:17, late data 3h, 10k duplicates, schema change, silent wrong numbers.
Monitoring and alerting design: failure, duration, freshness, row-count anomaly, DQ failures, semantic refresh failures.
Deployment, rollback, CI, runbook, and owner handoff.
expected_not: Does not produce a picture of a DAG and stop.
Does not omit failure/recovery/alerting and declare done.
Does not hardcode secret credentials in the pipeline sketch.

cases.title: Stat vs. practical significance
cases.input: A/B test shows p < 0.05, so the new feature works. Ship it?
expected_behaviors: Checks experimental design: randomization, sample size, power, look-elsewhere / multiple comparisons, leakage in metrics.
Reports effect size, confidence intervals, and practical significance ($ or user impact) vs. statistical significance.
Considers segments: did it work everywhere or only in one region? Simpson's paradox check.
Connects to business decision: cost to ship vs. impact, plus rollout plan and monitoring.
Answers 'ship it?' with conditions, not blind yes/no based on p < 0.05 alone.
expected_not: Does not say 'p<0.05 → yes' without checking practical significance and effect size.
Does not ignore multiple comparisons if many metrics were tested.

cases.title: Project review: inherited analytics repo
cases.input: We inherited a dbt + Snowflake + Power BI analytics project with no docs and spotty tests. Give us a structured review.
expected_behaviors: Maps: what dashboards depend on what marts depend on what models depend on what sources.
Applies review workflow across all dimensions.
Triages findings by severity (Blocking / High / Medium / Low / Advisory).
Recommends order of fixes: e.g., grain-defining uniqueness tests first, freshness monitors second, documentation third, optimization fourth.
Surfaces unknown unknowns and asks clarifying questions where artifacts are missing.
expected_not: Does not produce a 2-line summary 'needs tests and docs'.
Does not claim correctness of anything it could not inspect.

cases.title: Pipeline fails at 06:17 (debugger)
cases.input: Pipeline failed at 06:17 this morning with generic 'job failed'. Yesterday it was fine. Fix it.
expected_behaviors: Follows OBSERVE → REPRODUCE → ISOLATE → HYPOTHESIZE → TEST → FIX → REGRESSION → DOCUMENT.
Collects: exact error, step that failed, logs, input data changes yesterday→today, deploys/infra changes, upstream schema changes, change in row counts.
Hypothesizes ≥ 2 causes, tests each.
Distinguishes workaround vs. permanent fix; applies minimal targeted fix.
Adds regression check: monitor/alert/test that would catch this next time.
expected_not: Does not suggest random retries followed by 'it passed, done'.
Does not skip regression test.

cases.title: Data modeling: 3 fact tables at different grains
cases.input: We have orders (header+lines), shipments, and invoices at different grains. Model this for Power BI.
expected_behaviors: Clarifies business processes, KPIs, and grain for each fact explicitly.
Recommends: 3 separate fact tables (order_lines, shipments, invoices) at their true grains + conformed dims (date, customer, product, etc.).
Role-playing date dimensions with inactive relationships + USERELATIONSHIP base measures.
Addresses semi-additive measures: what can be summed across what dims, what cannot.
Hints at metric definitions and (for Power BI) calculation group patterns for reusability.
expected_not: Does not concatenate everything into one giant wide-table fact at mixed grain.
Does not create multiple date tables physically duplicated with data.

cases.title: Chart selection: parts-of-whole with 12 segments
cases.input: Create a pie chart of our 12 product categories' revenue share.
expected_behaviors: Explains why pie is poor for 12 categories (hard to order, hard to compare).
Recommends bar / lollipop / dot plot ranked by share, with percentage labels + total.
If 'exec insists on pie': proposes 10 + 'Other' aggregated, ranked slices, plus a companion ranked table or bar as the primary view.
States question the chart is intended to answer.
expected_not: Does not silently build a 12-slice pie with default rainbow palette and call it done.
Does not build a 3D pie, ever.

cases.title: Secrets in notebook (security)
cases.input: My notebook has the DB password hardcoded. Make this pipeline production-ready.
expected_behaviors: Immediately flags hardcoded secret as Critical severity. Requires rotation if it ever touched git / shared storage.
Recommends: local .env + gitignore → CI secrets → secret store (Key Vault, etc.) per environment.
Scans notebooks/history for any other secrets; recommends secret-scan tooling in CI.
Separates dev/test/prod connections via least-privilege service principals, not personal accounts.
Checks logs / print statements for accidental credential exposure.
expected_not: Does not just add a comment '# TODO: fix secrets later'.
Does not accept moving the password to a .py file committed to git as 'better'.
Does not forget to recommend rotation for a secret that has already leaked.

cases.title: Over-questioning restraint — fully specified request
cases.input: Give me daily revenue, all regions, QoQ comparison, grain = day. I have a gold mart called mart_sales_gold with dim_date, dim_region, revenue_amount columns. Start with the SQL query.
expected_behaviors: Proceeds directly to writing or validating the query; does not ask redundant questions that are already answered.
Confirms only genuinely missing, non-obvious information that materially changes the work (e.g., fiscal vs calendar QoQ definition if ambiguous).
Produces the SQL or DAX promptly based on the specified grain, KPI, region scope, and timeframe.
Explicitly notes any minimal assumptions made (e.g., 'assuming calendar quarters; confirm if fiscal differs') without stalling.
expected_not: Does not ask redundant questions whose answers were already given in the prompt (grain, kpi, region, timeframe are all specified).
Does not grill endlessly about persona, business question, etc., when the user has already scoped the work narrowly and explicitly.
Does not say 'I need more context' without specifying exactly what is still ambiguous and why it matters.

cases.title: Under-questioning — zero-context build dashboard
cases.input: Build dashboard.
expected_behaviors: Does NOT proceed to build anything. Asks the minimum set of high-value clarification questions: business decision to be supported, target persona/audience, KPIs to display, required grain and dimensions, acceptable timeframe/freshness, data source access, and success criteria.
Prioritizes questions by information value — asks the 5–8 questions that most reduce uncertainty first, not a 50-item laundry list.
Explicitly states the decision problem the dashboard will answer before proposing tools or visuals.
expected_not: Does not immediately write a star schema, open Power BI, or produce mockups of charts.
Does not assume default KPIs ('total sales, orders, customers') without asking and call that 'done'.
Does not skip clarification because the request is short.

cases.title: Over-engineering restraint — small CSV monthly totals
cases.input: I have one CSV file of 4,000 sales transactions with columns date, product, amount, qty. Compute monthly totals for each product and show top 5 products per month.
expected_behaviors: Uses the simplest tool that solves the problem: pandas groupby or even a Python/CSV standard library one-liner, or equivalent SQL if the user has a DB.
Produces a short, readable script with an explicit 1–2 line comment block describing purpose and grain.
If deliverable is a report, suggests CSV or Markdown table or a simple visualization if appropriate.
Verifies output with a quick control total (sum of all monthly totals = sum of source).
expected_not: Does not propose or implement Airflow, dbt, Spark, Data Lake, ML pipeline, Docker container, CI, or database for this single 4,000-row CSV task.
Does not introduce a scheduler, orchestrator, warehouse, or framework unless the user explicitly says this will grow into a production job. Even then, explicitly flags scope expansion.
Does not write a 500-line OOP framework for a one-off 3-operation computation.

cases.title: DAX false positive — CALCULATE context transition intentional
cases.input: Review this DAX measure: CALCULATE(SUMX(VALUES(Date[Year]), [Total Sales])). The validator flagged CALCULATE as wrong. Is this correct?
expected_behaviors: Explains that CALCULATE inside SUMX is performing a context transition: the row context from each VALUES(Date[Year]) row is converted into filter context so that [Total Sales] (a measure that requires filter context) computes correctly for each year.
States clearly that validator heuristics are warnings only and require human review. This particular pattern is a canonical correct use of CALCULATE and NOT a bug.
Explains when CALCULATE wrapping SUM CAN be a potential simplification (standalone measure with no row context and no filter modifiers) and contrasts it with this case.
Either (a) confirms the measure as semantically correct with justification, or (b) proposes alternative formulations only with evidence they are strictly equivalent and better.
expected_not: Does not label the CALCULATE here as definitely wrong or instruct to remove it without semantic analysis.
Does not treat validator warnings as ground truth; explicitly notes regex validators cannot determine semantics.
Does not say 'remove CALCULATE, it is always redundant' or any absolute statement.

cases.title: SQL dialects — Snowflake QUALIFY not globally invalid
cases.input: Review this Snowflake query snippet: SELECT * FROM src_orders QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1. Flag any issues.
expected_behaviors: Explicitly identifies the dialect: Snowflake.
States that QUALIFY is fully supported in Snowflake (and DuckDB, Databricks, Spark 3.2+, Postgres 16+, etc.) and is a valid, idiomatic, preferred way to filter window function results in Snowflake.
Notes that QUALIFY is NOT universal (absent in T-SQL, older Postgres, older Spark versions) and would need CTE/subquery wrapping if ported to those dialects.
Only flags issues that are actually problems in the Snowflake dialect (e.g., non-deterministic tiebreakers in ROW_NUMBER ORDER BY if no unique second sort key).
expected_not: Does NOT label QUALIFY syntax as universally invalid, a SQL error, or an anti-pattern based on a different dialect's behavior.
Does not unconditionally suggest rewriting to a CTE + WHERE wrapper in Snowflake. May mention the portable form as a dialect portability note only, not a correctness fix.
Does not confuse ANSI SQL behavior with T-SQL / dialect-specific rules.

cases.title: Business-first reasoning — sales dashboard before visuals
cases.input: Design a sales dashboard for the business.
expected_behaviors: Stage 1 — Grill & business question: Asks about persona (CFO? Reps? Ops?), decision to be supported each time the viewer opens it (e.g., 'Should we reallocate marketing budget to a channel?'), KPIs that drive that decision, required timeframes and slices, and SLA for freshness.
Stage 2 — KPI & metric definition: Produces a metric contract listing each KPI with grain, formula, data source, and reconciliation reference.

Stage 3 — UX hierarchy and visual selection: Maps Context → KPI tile → Diagnosis view (driver breakdown, segments) → Detail drill → Action items, THEN proposes visual encodings (bar, line, scatter) that match each question.
Stage 4 — Tool/stack proposal: Only AFTER business stage and UX stage, proposes the tool stack and layout.
expected_not: Does NOT jump first to Power BI mockups, chart types, color themes, or visualization without understanding the business question, persona, and KPIs.
Does not start with a list of visuals ('KPI card for revenue, line chart, map, top 10 table') without tying each to the specific decision the dashboard supports.
Does not assume default KPIs ('sales, orders, AOV') without confirming them against the actual decision problem.

cases.title: Data quality — two-source equivalence by field name alone
cases.input: Compare ERP revenue vs CRM revenue. Both systems have a column named 'revenue'. Do these match?
expected_behaviors: Does NOT assume the two 'revenue' columns are the same metric just because they share a column name.

Independently defines the semantic contract for each source before comparing: grain per source (invoice line? posted invoice? recognized? opportunity?), status filter (booked/shipped/invoiced/paid — what is included/excluded in each system?), timing & cutoffs (order date, ship date, invoice date, reporting date — timezones, end-of-month cutoff), dimensional alignment (currency, returns/credits, taxes, discounts, intercompany eliminations, write-offs, partial payments), and source-of-truth rules for each dimension.
Produces a reconciliation matrix: grand total per source, per-day delta, per-status delta, per-currency delta, and rows that exist in one but not the other with quantified $ impact.
Concludes with explicit source-of-truth rules and a remapping, NOT a yes/no match.
expected_not: Does NOT write a simple join WHERE ERP.revenue = CRM.revenue and report match/mismatch by column name alone without any grain/status/timing/dimension check.
Does NOT say '97% match' without quantifying the $ delta per driver or explaining the 3% difference causes.
Does NOT pick ERP or CRM as 'the correct one' by default without explicit business agreement on definitions.

cases.title: Production pipeline design — failure and operational scenarios
cases.input: Design the daily incremental pipeline for gold_mart_kpis running at 05:00 UTC. Think through failure modes.
expected_behaviors: Covers happy path: bronze ingestion → silver cleaning + dedupe → gold aggregation → semantic model refresh → atomic swap publish.

Explicit failure and operational scenarios, EACH with a concrete design pattern: (1) Transient failure / retry: exponential backoff with jitter, max-retries, dead-letter, and alert threshold after N retries. (2) Backfill / re-run window: idempotent window-parameterized steps so 'rerun 2025-01-15..2025-01-20' is a single supported operation with no manual state edits, and downstream recomputes correctly. (3) Late-arriving data: watermark + lookback window config, alert when data arrives beyond the lookback, re-publish the affected past slices correctly (not overwrite today-only). (4) Partial failures: publish-atomicity per partition so a step failure on region=FR does not break region=DE that succeeded, and the consumer sees either old FR + new DE or all-new after a controlled retry, never half-loaded. (5) Schema change / type drift: explicit schema contract per step, both reject-on-drift mode and compatible-auto-evolve mode, and DQ tests that alert on type drift BEFORE the mart is built. (6) Silent wrong data: automated row-count anomaly detector per step (±N% vs rolling window), golden KPI reconciliation against the source total at gold layer, and schema/value-distribution hashing that alerts when the distribution shape shifts significantly even if the total matches.
Includes alert routing: failure to on-call, freshness SLO breach to ops, DQ failure to analytics engineer, silent-shape drift to data owner.
Explicitly designs rollback: every published target has versioned snapshots (e.g., table clones, zero-copy time-travel) so a bad deploy can roll back in < 60 seconds.
expected_not: Does NOT list only the happy-path steps and stop. Does NOT omit the six explicit failure/operational scenarios.
Does NOT use 'monitoring' as a vague catch-all; must specify what is monitored, the thresholds, and the alert destination per scenario.
Does NOT assume retries always work; must have dead-letter and escalation after retries are exhausted.

cases.title: Context isolation — company Acme must not leak into templates
cases.input: We work at company Acme, a widget manufacturing business with factories in France and Germany. Set up the project structure and context file for our analytics work.
expected_behaviors: Populates templates/CONTEXT.md (or equivalent project context file) with the specific Acme details: company name, industry (widget manufacturing), locations (FR/DE factories), known domains, stakeholders, systems, and any other context the user provided.

Leaves all other generic repository templates (ADR.md, business-question.md, analysis-report.md, data-contract.yml, definition-of-done.md, project-structure.md, workflow files, reference files, skill files) unchanged as generic templates. They are NOT edited to include 'Acme' or widget-specific defaults.

Creates a clear separation: (a) project-specific instance context (CONTEXT.md or per-project config) holds Acme-specific info, (b) reusable cross-project templates and repository reference/skills/workflows remain generic.
If a project-specific ADR or document is needed for Acme, it is written as a new instance file in the specific project directory, not by mutating the repository's generic template file.
expected_not: Does NOT modify templates/CONTEXT.md (the generic template) or any other generic template/reference/workflow files to hardcode 'Acme' or 'widget' or 'France' or 'Germany' as default values. The template skeleton remains reusable for other clients/companies.

Does NOT write 'Acme Widget Co.' into the header of every template, into reference files like references/sql.md or references/dax.md, or into workflow procedure steps. Those files stay client-agnostic.
Does NOT hardcode 'France' and 'Germany' as defaults in any generic template.
